terms.grammar: interrogative adverb, in direct and indirect questions
evidence: Cic. Fam. 16.18.3: tē quandō exspectēmus fac ut sciam
terms.comment: Asks for the time of a thing. The conjunction “when” (“when he came, …”) is a different record.
See “how long ago?”; for the hour, “at what time?”.

phrases.english: When? — Today. — How long ago? — Just now.

phrases.latin: crās tē vīctūrum, crās dīcis, Postume, semper: dīc mihi, crās istud, Postume, quandō venit?
phrases.english: Tomorrow you will live, you always say, Postumus, tomorrow: tell me, Postumus, when does that tomorrow come?

phrases.latin: tē quandō exspectēmus fac ut sciam. cūrā tē dīligenter. valē.
phrases.english: Let me know when we should expect you. Look after yourself. Goodbye.

phrases.latin: Quandō vīs venī, parāta rēs erit. — Properā modo.
phrases.english: Come when you like, it will be ready. — Just hurry.

quando.html: De Vaan 507, s.v. quī, gives the final vowel long; Festus records an older quandōd (Lewis & Short s.v. quando). Shortened to quando in later verse. As in aliquandō (see “ever”); the libellī write quandō.

sources: Lewis & Short: quando · Lewis & Short: dudum (quam dudum)
